# Brief: rebuild the weekend rota so it stops falling on the same six people

The weekend rota has drifted into something nobody designed. Six people cover
most of it, three of them cover most of that, and the rest of the department has
not worked a Saturday in over a year. I want it rebuilt before the winter
period, and I want the rebuild to survive contact with the next three months
rather than lasting until the first swap request.

## Background

The rota was written when the department was eleven people and the weekend was
one person on call and one in the building. We are now twenty-six, the weekend
carries a full despatch shift, and the rota has been extended rather than
rewritten each time: a column added here, a name pencilled in there, and a
private arrangement between two people that has outlived both of their job
titles.

The result is a document that is technically accurate and practically fiction.
The published version says the load is shared. The lived version is that the
same six absorb every gap, partly because they are reliable and partly because
asking them is faster than asking anybody else.

## What I want from this piece of work

- An honest picture of who has actually worked which weekends over the last
  twelve months. Not the rota as published — the hours as worked, from the door
  system if that is the only record that did not get edited afterwards.
- A rebuilt pattern that spreads the load across everybody who is contracted for
  it, with the exceptions named rather than implied. Two people have caring
  arrangements the department has always worked around, and that should be
  written down as a decision rather than continuing as a habit nobody can
  explain to a newcomer.
- A swap mechanism that does not quietly undo the balancing the moment it is
  used. The current arrangement is a group chat, and a swap agreed there is
  invisible to the published rota, so the published rota is wrong within a week
  of every rewrite.
- A view on whether the weekend needs the headcount it currently has. Two of the
  six say the second person on Sunday has nothing to do after eleven. If that is
  true, the balancing problem is smaller than it looks and the fix is partly
  scheduling and partly staffing.

## Constraints

The pattern has to work with the annual leave already approved, which is heavier
than usual in February. It has to keep two named people off the same weekend —
they cover each other's specialisms and the department cannot lose both at once.
And it has to be something the supervisors can run without me, which rules out
anything that needs a spreadsheet only one person understands.

## What I do not want

I do not want a fairness score. The last attempt at this produced a weighted
model with a coefficient for unsociable hours, and the argument moved from who
works weekends to whether the coefficient was right. Count the weekends, show
the counts, and let people argue about the counts.

## Deliverable

A one-page pattern, the twelve months of history that justifies it, and a short
note on the two exceptions and why they stand. Bring it to the supervisors'
meeting rather than sending it round first — the alignment we need is in the
room, not in a reply-all.
